endorsements.title: Adoption of AI in Healthcare Delivery Systems: Early Applications and Impacts
endorsements.quote: Any strategy focused on reducing administrative burden must deeply understand what existing workflows they are replacing, reorganizing, or augmenting with AI-based solutions.

endorsements.title: Policy brief: ambient AI scribes and the coding arms race
endorsements.quote: A clear, nontechnical disclosure that an AI assistant records to help the clinician document the visit —and that the clinician reviews and controls the note—can protect trust without derailing care12.

endorsements.title: Barriers and opportunities of scaling ambient AI scribes for clinical documentation across diverse healthcare settings
endorsements.quote: Protocols should define when ambient listening is appropriate, ensure patients are informed and provide consent to recording, and establish alternative processes for those who decline, ensuring their care remains timely and unaffected 48 .

endorsements.title: The ethics of listening walls: patient autonomy and consent in the age of ambient clinical AI
endorsements.quote: Patients should receive clear verbal and written explanations that clinical encounters may be recorded using AI systems for documentation, alongside transparent information about how audio and text data will be stored, accessed, and used.

endorsements.title: The Utility and Implications of Ambient Scribes in Primary Care
endorsements.quote: The physician (or another team member in the clinic) may be required to obtain consent from the patient to use the ambient scribe and answer questions about the technology.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Scribe and Large Language Model Technology in Healthcare Documentation: Advantages, Limitations, and Recommendations
endorsements.issuer: Plastic and reconstructive surgery. Global open
endorsements.quote: As good practice, prior written informed consent should be obtained before using any type of AI scribe.

endorsements.title: AI-augmented frameworks for enhancing Alzheimer's disease clinical trials: A memory clinic perspective
endorsements.issuer: The journal of prevention of Alzheimer's disease
endorsements.quote: Consent should occur at multiple steps: for non-standard assessments (e.g., digital biomarkers or speech analysis) that may inform models beyond immediate care; an explicit opt-in for trial eligibility screening, with disclosures on procedures specific to recruitment to avoid therapeutic misconception; and a separate consent for aggregating de-identified data with others for research purposes.

endorsements.title: AI Scribe Use in Residency Training: A Call for Specialty Society Guidance in Graduate Medical Education
endorsements.issuer: Advances in medical education and practice
endorsements.quote: Such policies should incorporate mandatory resident review and note sign-off of AI-generated notes, clear accountability protocols, patient consent standards, and limitations on use depending on the note section such as formulation of assessment and plan.

endorsements.title: The Ethics Committee of the Italian Society of Anesthesia, Analgesia, Resuscitation and Intensive Care (SIAARTI) - Artificial intelligence in end-of-life decision-making processes: ethical reflections
endorsements.issuer: Journal of anesthesia, analgesia and critical care
endorsements.quote: Second, it should be noted that any documentation (audio or video) of clinical conversations would necessarily require the patient’s full awareness, based on clear and comprehensive information, and explicit, documented consent.

endorsements.title: Artificial intelligence-assisted mental healthcare in general practice: Benefits, risks and future possibilities
endorsements.quote: For instance, if consultations will be recorded for an AI scribe, the patient must agree to that recording, knowing who will have access to the audio or transcript.

endorsements.title: Using ambient AI in clinical consultations: reframing policy around clinical audit and patient safety
endorsements.quote: Under the GDPR, explicit consent will often be required, or will be the most appropriate lawful basis, for consultation recording in the use we propose; the precise lawful basis must nonetheless be determined under applicable national law and institutional arrangements, and consent to recording remains distinct both from consent to care and from the lawful basis for any subsequent processing ( 6 ).

endorsements.title: The Promise of Ambient AI Technology in Medical Education: Opportunities and Guardrails
endorsements.quote: Teach explicit, repeatable patient consent scripts as a clinical skill.

evidence.outcome: GP consent practices before using ambient scribe to record consultations
evidence.effect: 63% (n=89) routinely sought consent, with ≤10% of patients declining; practices varied.

evidence.title: Patient attitudes toward ambient artificial intelligence scribes in clinical care: insights from a cross-sectional study
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.outcome: Patient awareness of AI scribe use
evidence.effect: Awareness of AI scribe use was low (28.3%); 61.8% were reluctant about future AI scribe use, and privacy concerns were linked to lower odds of future use (aOR = 0.65).
evidence.quote: Awareness of AI scribe use was low (28.3%).

commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether obtaining consent before ambient AI scribe use protects patient privacy or trust, although nine sources endorse the practice. Surveys from New Zealand and the United Kingdom show that roughly 4 in 10 scribe users did not report routinely seeking consent.

perspectives.view: Three descriptive surveys document the hazard, and none compares consent with no consent or measures outcomes such as privacy complaints or trust. The nine endorsements are guidance and commentary, and the recommendation rests on expert opinion and legal reasoning. Certainty about effect cannot be rated because no test of the practice exists.

In New Zealand, 59% of AI scribe users reported seeking consent. In the United Kingdom, 63% of GP users routinely did so. These figures suggest that unconsented recording occurs in routine care. The surveys do not show whether a consent step, once adopted, is completed reliably at each visit.

UK GPs reported varied consent practices, and they reported that 10% or fewer of patients declined when asked. This suggests that asking may lead few patients to refuse. No study measured the time a consent script takes, whether documented consent persists across visits, or how often clinicians skip the step when clinics are busy.

The UK decline rate of 10% or fewer implies that a small share of visits will need a non-scribe documentation path. One endorsing commentary calls for alternative processes so that patients who decline still receive timely care. No study reports the staffing or cost of running consent and fallback workflows at scale.

Among 12,153 Canadian adults, 28.3% were aware of AI scribe use and 61.8% were reluctant about future use. Privacy concerns were linked to lower odds of future use (aOR = 0.65). This may mean that many patients do not know when they are being recorded. Whether asking for consent changes trust has not been studied.

One endorsing commentary states that explicit consent will often be required under the GDPR, with the lawful basis set by national law. The supplied studies come from New Zealand, the United Kingdom, and Canada. None examines compliance with a specific legal consent requirement or its enforcement.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares consent processes, such as verbal versus written or per-visit versus standing consent, against no consent. Patient trust, privacy complaints, clinician burden, and whether patients understand what they agreed to have not been measured in any test of consent. Decline rates have been reported only as GP estimates in one UK survey, and no study compares them across consent methods.
commentary.underserved_note: None of the three surveys reports results for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and no study tested the practice in any group. As a result, nothing is known about whether consent scripts are understood by patients with limited English or low literacy, or whether decline rates and fallback care differ in these groups.
